title: Ribosome
body: Non-membrane subcellular structures made of rRNA and protein, found in all forms of life, that synthesize proteins according to mRNA sequences.
ced_evidence: 2.1.A.1 "Ribosomes synthesize proteins according to messenger RNA (mRNA) sequences"

title: Components of the endomembrane system
body: Membrane-bound organelles and subcellular components that work together to modify, package, and transport polysaccharides, lipids, and proteins.
ced_evidence: 2.1.A.2 "endoplasmic reticulum (ER), Golgi complex, lysosomes, vacuoles and transport vesicles, the nuclear envelope, and the plasma membrane"

title: Rough ER
body: Endoplasmic reticulum associated with membrane-bound ribosomes that allows compartmentalization of the cell and helps carry out protein synthesis.
ced_evidence: 2.1.A.3.i "Rough ER is associated with membrane-bound ribosomes"

title: Smooth ER
body: Endoplasmic reticulum whose functions include detoxification of cells and lipid synthesis.
ced_evidence: 2.1.A.3.ii "detoxification of cells and lipid synthesis"

title: Endoplasmic reticulum (general roles)
body: Provides mechanical support by helping cells maintain shape and plays a role in intracellular transport.
ced_evidence: 2.1.A.3 "helping cells maintain shape and plays a role in intracellular transport"

title: Golgi complex
body: A membrane-bound structure of flattened membrane sacs that correctly folds and chemically modifies newly synthesized cellular products and packages proteins for trafficking.
ced_evidence: 2.1.A.4 "series of flattened membrane sacs"; illustrative example: glycosylation and other chemical modifications

title: Mitochondria
body: Double-membrane organelles whose compartments hold different metabolic reactions of aerobic cellular respiration; the smooth outer membrane surrounds a highly convoluted inner membrane whose folds enable more efficient ATP synthesis.
ced_evidence: 2.1.A.5 "inner membrane is highly convoluted, forming folds that enable ATP to be synthesized more efficiently"

title: Lysosome
body: Membrane-enclosed sac containing hydrolytic enzymes that digest material and that plays a role in programmed cell death (apoptosis).
ced_evidence: 2.1.A.6 "hydrolytic enzymes that digest material"

title: Vacuole (plant vs. animal)
body: Membrane-bound sac; a plant cell's specialized large vacuole maintains turgor pressure through nutrient and water storage, while animal-cell vacuoles are smaller, more plentiful, and store cellular materials.
ced_evidence: 2.1.A.7 "maintains turgor pressure through nutrient and water storage"

title: Chloroplast
body: Double-membrane organelle found in plants and photosynthetic algae that serves as the location for photosynthesis.
ced_evidence: 2.1.A.8 "serve as the location for photosynthesis"

title: Volume of a sphere
ced_evidence: 2.2.A.1 Relevant Equations: Volume of a Sphere

title: Volume of a cube
ced_evidence: 2.2.A.1 Relevant Equations: Volume of a Cube

title: Volume of a rectangular solid
body: V = lwh
ced_evidence: 2.2.A.1 Relevant Equations: Volume of a Rectangular Solid: V = lwh

title: Volume of a cylinder
body: V = \pi r^{2} h
ced_evidence: 2.2.A.1 Relevant Equations: Volume of a Cylinder

title: Surface area of a sphere
body: SA = 4\pi r^{2}
ced_evidence: 2.2.A.1 Relevant Equations: Surface Area of a Sphere

title: Surface area of a cube
ced_evidence: 2.2.A.1 Relevant Equations: Surface Area of a Cube: SA = 6s^2

title: Surface area of a rectangular solid
body: SA = 2lh + 2lw + 2wh
ced_evidence: 2.2.A.1 Relevant Equations: SA = 2lh + 2lw + 2wh

title: Surface area of a cylinder
body: SA = 2\pi r h + 2\pi r^{2}
ced_evidence: 2.2.A.1 Relevant Equations: Surface Area of a Cylinder

title: Cell size and surface area-to-volume ratio
body: As cells increase in volume, the surface area-to-volume ratio decreases and demand for internal resources increases, so smaller cells typically have a higher ratio and more efficient exchange with the environment.
ced_evidence: 2.2.A.2.i-ii "As cells increase in volume, the surface area-to-volume ratio decreases"

title: Size, heat exchange, and metabolic rate
body: As an organism's mass increases, its surface area-to-volume ratio and rate of heat exchange decrease, and smaller multicellular organisms typically have a higher metabolic rate per unit body mass.
ced_evidence: 2.2.A.2.iv-v "the smaller the organism, the higher the metabolic rate per unit body mass"

title: Membrane folds compensate for low SA:V
body: More complex cellular structures, such as membrane folds, are necessary to adequately exchange materials with the environment.
ced_evidence: 2.2.A.2.iii "More complex cellular structures (e.g., membrane folds)"

title: Phospholipid orientation in the membrane
body: The polar hydrophilic phosphate regions face the aqueous external or internal environment, while the nonpolar hydrophobic fatty acid regions face each other in the membrane interior.
ced_evidence: 2.3.A.1 "nonpolar hydrophobic fatty acid regions face each other within the interior of the membrane"

title: Orientation of embedded protein regions
body: Hydrophilic protein regions are inside the protein or exposed to the cytosol, and hydrophobic regions form the protein surface that interacts with the fatty acids in the membrane interior.
ced_evidence: 2.3.A.2.i-ii "Hydrophobic regions of proteins make up the protein surface that interacts with the fatty acids"

title: Fluid mosaic model
body: A model of the plasma membrane as a structural framework of phospholipids embedded with proteins, steroids, glycoproteins, and glycolipids that can all move around the surface of the cell within the membrane.
ced_evidence: 2.3.B.1 "as illustrated by the fluid mosaic model"

title: Fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane
body: Labelled parts of the membrane diagram students must read and describe.

items.label: Phospholipid bilayer
items.meaning: Hydrophilic phosphate regions face aqueous surroundings; hydrophobic fatty acid tails face each other in the interior

items.label: Embedded proteins
items.meaning: Hydrophilic, hydrophobic, or both; hydrophobic regions contact the fatty acids

items.label: Glycoproteins
items.meaning: Embedded components that move within the membrane

items.label: Glycolipids
items.meaning: Embedded components that move within the membrane

ced_evidence: 2.3.B.1 "phospholipid molecules embedded with proteins, steroids (such as cholesterol in vertebrate animals), glycoproteins, and glycolipids"

title: Selective permeability
body: The property of the plasma membrane, resulting from its hydrophobic interior, that lets some substances cross while restricting others.
ced_evidence: 2.4.A.1 "Selective permeability is the result of the plasma membrane having a hydrophobic interior"

title: What crosses the membrane and how
body: Membrane passage depends on molecule size, polarity, and charge.

items.label: Large polar molecules and ions
items.meaning: Move through embedded channels and transport proteins

caution: Nonpolar hydrocarbon tails prevent ions and polar molecules from crossing on their own, so cite the hydrophobic interior in an explanation.
ced_evidence: 2.4.A.2-3 "Small nonpolar molecules, including N2, O2, and CO2, freely pass across the membrane"

title: Cell wall
body: A structure in Bacteria, Archaea, Fungi, and plants that provides a structural boundary, a permeability barrier for some substances, and protection from osmotic lysis.
ced_evidence: 2.4.B.1 "protection from osmotic lysis"

title: Passive transport
body: The net movement of molecules from regions of high concentration to regions of low concentration without the direct input of metabolic energy.
ced_evidence: 2.5.A.2 "without the direct input of metabolic energy"

title: Active transport
body: Transport that requires the direct input of energy to move molecules, in some cases from regions of low concentration to regions of high concentration.
ced_evidence: 2.5.A.3 "requires the direct input of energy"

title: Endocytosis
body: An energy-requiring process in which the cell takes in large molecules and particulate matter by folding the plasma membrane in on itself and forming small vesicles that engulf material from the external environment.
caution: Endocytosis and exocytosis both require energy to move large substances into and out of cells.
ced_evidence: 2.5.B.1.i "folding the plasma membrane in on itself and forming new (small) vesicles"

title: Facilitated diffusion
body: Movement through transport or channel proteins, including charged ions and large polar molecules, down the concentration gradient with no energy input.
ced_evidence: 2.6.A.1-2 "Facilitated diffusion enables the movement of large polar molecules through membranes with no energy input"

title: Aquaporin
body: A membrane protein that transports large quantities of water across membranes.
ced_evidence: 2.6.A.3 "Aquaporins transport large quantities of water across membranes"

title: Ions need channel proteins; ion movement can polarize membranes
body: Charged ions such as Na+ and K+ require channel proteins to cross the membrane, and their movement across it may polarize the membrane.
ced_evidence: 2.6.A.1.i-ii "Charged ions, including Na+ (sodium) and K+ (potassium), require channel proteins"

title: Tonicity of the external environment
body: External environments can be hypotonic, hypertonic, or isotonic to the internal environment of cells.

items.label: Hypotonic
items.meaning: External environment relative to the cell; water moves hypotonic to hypertonic

items.label: Hypertonic
items.meaning: External environment relative to the cell; water moves hypotonic to hypertonic

items.label: Isotonic
items.meaning: External environment relative to the cell

caution: State direction relative to the cell's internal environment and describe water movement by osmosis.
ced_evidence: 2.7.A.1 "hypotonic, hypertonic, or isotonic to internal environments of cells"

title: Direction of osmosis
body: Water moves by osmosis from regions of high water potential to regions of low water potential, which is the same as moving from low solute concentration (low osmolarity) to high solute concentration (high osmolarity).
ced_evidence: 2.7.A.1 and 2.7.B.2 "from regions of low osmolarity or solute concentration to regions of high osmolarity"

title: Water potential
body: \Psi = \Psi_{P} + \Psi_{S}
ced_evidence: 2.7.A.1 Relevant Equation: Water Potential, Ψp = pressure potential, Ψs = solute potential

title: Solute potential of a solution
body: \Psi_{S} = -iCRT
ced_evidence: 2.7.B.2 Relevant Equation: s = −iCRT

title: Variables in the solute potential equation
body: Terms in Ψs = −iCRT with the CED's constant and units.
ced_evidence: 2.7.B.2 "i = ionization constant; C = molar concentration; R = pressure constant; T = temperature in Kelvin (°C + 273)"

title: Osmoregulation
body: The maintenance of water balance that allows organisms to control their internal solute composition and water potential.
ced_evidence: 2.7.B.2 "Osmoregulation maintains water balance and allows organisms to control their internal solute composition and water potential"

title: Na+/K+ pump
body: A membrane protein that uses metabolic energy (ATP) for active transport and helps maintain the membrane potential and electrochemical gradients.
ced_evidence: 2.8.A.1.ii "The Na+/K+ pump and ATPase contribute to the maintenance of the membrane potential"

title: How internal membranes aid compartmentalization
body: Internal membranes and membrane-bound organelles facilitate cellular processes in two ways.

items.label: Minimizing competing interactions
items.meaning: Separates metabolic processes and specific enzymatic reactions

items.label: Increasing surface area
items.meaning: Provides more membrane surface where reactions can occur

ced_evidence: 2.9.B.1 "minimizing competing interactions and by increasing the surface area where reactions can occur"

title: Endosymbiosis
body: The process by which membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria and chloroplasts evolved from once free-living prokaryotic cells.
ced_evidence: 2.10.A.1 "evolved from once free-living prokaryotic cells via endosymbiosis"

title: Compartmentalization: prokaryotes vs. eukaryotes
body: Comparison of internal organization in prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

items.label: Prokaryotes
items.meaning: Typically lack internal membrane-bound organelles but have internal regions with specialized structures and functions

items.label: Eukaryotes
items.meaning: Maintain internal membranes that partition the cell into specialized regions

ced_evidence: 2.10.A.2-3 "Prokaryotes typically lack internal membrane-bound organelles"
